prize_parts.citation: for empirical and conceptual analyses of how technology and import competition reshape labour demand, local labour markets and wage inequality

statement.case_for: My opening first choice was B014 and my second was B022. Having read colleagues' maturity arguments, I now put B022 first. The China-shock studies and the task-based account of technology answer a big question with credible quasi-experimental designs. They also fit my own standard that new evidence together with an explanatory framework makes a contribution. The shock designs are transparent, and the papers span roughly two decades, so replication, critique and refinement have had time to occur. The persistent local adjustment costs they document are a first-order finding for labour economics, trade and public policy. The Autor-Dorn-Hanson trio is also the cleanest attribution for the trade-shock evidence, and Autor anchors the task strand. Among the shortlisted candidates, B022 combines wide cross-member standing with an attributable credit set.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the China-shock magnitudes, long-run persistence and shift-share identification remain contested. The task framework also has intellectual roots (Acemoglu, Levy, Murnane and others) outside the credited set, and the 2024 prize on technology and institutions is thematically close. A prize built on this ballot risks crediting the empirical programme while leaving out part of the theory that frames it.

responses.point: B014 is less mature than the other top candidates. Its main results date from 2014-2022, replication and long-run follow-up are still accumulating, and the causal reading of place effects is under scrutiny.
responses.response: This is a fair point, and it is the main reason I moved B014 from first to an alternative. I still think the mobility atlases and exposure-effect designs have been replicated across settings and are of prize quality. But on timing, B022's evidence base is simply older and has been tested harder by critics. I would not abandon B014 and would revisit it once the neighbourhood-effects replications are further along. I disagree that the maturity gap makes B014 weak on substance. It is a question of sequencing.

responses.point: A two-person prize for Autor and Hanson is cleaner. Dorn and Katz are more junior or tied to other bodies of work, and the task-framework credit is diffuse.
responses.response: I agree that Katz should not be on this prize. His strongest claims are the earlier skill-premium and education-technology work and the Moving to Opportunity work that belongs to B014. I would keep Dorn. He is a co-author on the core China-shock papers, so dropping him leaves the trade-shock attribution looking arbitrary. The task-framework credit is not made cleaner by a two-name cut, because the missing originators sit outside the ballot anyway. A citation that stresses labour-market adjustment to technology and trade fits the Autor-Dorn-Hanson set.

responses.point: Autor, Hanson and Katz is a defensible trio, with Dorn as the main alternative, since Katz is central to the earlier skill-premium and technology-race literature.
responses.response: I see the logic, but I would qualify it. Katz's central contributions mostly predate and are separate from the China-shock programme. Including him changes the subject of the prize from adjustment to trade and technology shocks to the broader skill-supply story, and that would blur the citation. Dorn's role in the shock evidence is directly attributable. I also note that Katz appears in B014, so crediting him there is a cleaner use of his record if the Committee wants to recognise him at all.

responses.point: The China-shock contribution is clearly attributable to Autor, Dorn and Hanson, but the task framework has wider origins, and the debate over effect sizes continues.
responses.response: I agree on both points and would build the citation around what is clearly attributable, namely the empirical analysis of how technology and import competition reshape labour demand and local labour markets, rather than claiming the task framework as a whole. On effect sizes, the debate concerns the magnitude and persistence of the shocks, not their direction. The finding that adjustment is slow and costly has survived several reanalyses, as far as I can judge from the openings.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee frames the award around the task framework or the trade-shock evidence, and how much the 2024 prize on technology and institutions narrows the room for it.
How far the China-shock magnitudes and persistence hold up under shift-share identification critiques, which I cannot settle from the supplied evidence.
Whether B014's recency is a genuine scientific reservation or only a timing one, and whether Katz or Friedman should be named if B014 is pursued.
Whether the three-name cap leaves out originators of the task framework who are not on the ballot.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. I work in labour economics and the economics of crime, which is adjacent to B014 and B022, but the listed frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler) are not among the credited names on the shortlisted ballots.
